question: What does f do to the simplest, most varied single inputs — plain words, mixed case, digits, symbols, and spaces — so I can see whether it is identity, case-changing, reversing, encoding, or something else?
expect: With no model, this broad baseline tells me the basic transformation. If outputs equal inputs, f may be identity on these. If case flips or normalizes, I'll see it in hello/Hello/HELLO. If order reverses, abc/xyz will show cba/zyx. If symbols/digits are filtered or encoded, a1!B2? and !@#$% will reveal it. If spaces are altered, 'two words' and '  spaced  ' will differ visibly.

question: Does f treat letters that are not at the very end (e.g. last letter before trailing punctuation/digits, or letters inside the string) specially, or is the final character really the only thing that matters?
expect: Model predicts final-character-only rule: abc!->abc!, abc1->abc1, 'abc '->'abc ', ab!c->ab!d, a1c->a1d, 'ab c'->'ab d', AbC->AbD, zZ->zA, ZZ->ZA, 9z->9a. If any output instead increments the last *letter* (e.g. abc!->abd!, abc1->abd1, 'abc '->abd ), that reveals f skips trailing non-letters. If uppercase/lowercase or the z->a wrap behaves differently (zZ->za, ZZ->ZZ), that reveals case or wrap rules beyond what E1 showed.

question: Does f act only on the final character, or does it also transform letters elsewhere when the last character is a non-letter (e.g., trailing digit/space/symbol), and does it handle empty strings and longer words consistently?
expect: If the model is right, outputs will be: 'a', 'A', 'ba', 'aA', 'ZA', 'aa', 'hello world!', 'Hello World!', 'abc123', 'abc '. Any deviation—especially changes to earlier letters when the last char is non-letter, or different handling of single letters/case—would reveal additional operations beyond incrementing only the final alphabetic character.

question: Does f still advance the final letter when the string mixes scripts or contains non-ASCII letters (accented, Greek, Cyrillic, emoji, Unicode whitespace), i.e. is the 'letter' test strictly ASCII a-z/A-Z or Unicode-aware?
expect: If f's letter test is strictly ASCII a-z/A-Z, then only strings ending in an ASCII letter change: 'café'->'café' (é unchanged), 'naïve'->'naïve', 'αβγ'->'αβγ', 'привет'->'привет', 'aé'->'aé', 'éa'->'éb', 'ß'->'ß', 'aß'->'aß', 'x😀'->'x😀', and 'abc\u00a0'->'abc\u00a0'. If it is Unicode-aware, accented/Greek/Cyrillic final letters would advance (e.g. 'café'->'cafê', 'αβγ'->'αβδ', 'привет'->'привет' or 'привеу' depending on alphabet handling), which would show the model's ASCII-only rule is incomplete.

question: Is the final-character 'advance' Unicode-aware for accented Latin letters (é->ê, ß->à), and does it follow Unicode code-point order rather than ASCII?
expect: If Unicode-aware with code-point+1: é->ê, è->é, à->á, ç->è, ñ->ò, ü->ý, ÿ->Ā (multi-char?), ß->à, þ->ÿ, œ->Ĕ. If it only advances within some limited alphabet mapping, results will differ (e.g., ÿ or ß unchanged, or wrapping). This pins down whether the rule is 'last char code point + 1' generally or a special-cased accented-letter table.

question: Does the 'advance the final character' rule apply to non-letter Unicode categories beyond letters — e.g. digits (ASCII and other scripts), symbols, punctuation, and combining marks — or does it leave all non-letter final characters unchanged as the model assumes?
expect: Model predicts all unchanged (a5, a٥, a², a+, a、, a€, a+combining, a\t, a\u200b, a½). If any come back advanced (e.g. a5->a6, a²->a³, a+->a, or the combining mark increments), then the rule is broader than 'alphabetic' — it may be 'any non-space character' or 'any character whose code point has a successor in the same category'. Each advanced case reveals the true category test; all-unchanged confirms non-letters are left alone.

question: Does the Unicode code-point increment apply to final letters at the top of the BMP (e.g. U+FF5A fullwidth z, U+FFFF) and does it produce a surrogate-pair character (astral plane) when incrementing U+FFFD or similar, and what happens at the very end of the BMP?
expect: If the rule is a pure chr(ord(last)+1) for any isalpha() final char, then U+FF5A (fullwidth z, a letter) -> U+FF5B, U+FF21 (fullwidth A) -> U+FF22, U+FFFD (replacement char, not a letter) unchanged, U+FFFF (noncharacter, not a letter) unchanged, U+D7FF (not a letter) unchanged, U+4E2D (CJK letter) -> U+4E2E. Any deviation (e.g. astral output, wrap, unchanged letter) reveals a boundary in the advance rule.

question: Does the final-character rule apply when the string ends in an astral-plane letter (e.g. Deseret/Gothic letters above U+FFFF), and if so does it increment by code point (possibly crossing into a non-letter), or does it treat astral characters as non-letters and leave them unchanged?
expect: If astral letters are advanced by code point, U+10400 (Deseret capital long I) -> U+10401, U+10427 (Deseret capital Z) -> U+10428 (which is a lowercase Deseret letter, revealing pure code-point increment with no case preservation), and U+1D400 (math bold A) -> U+1D401. If the box only recognizes BMP letters (as current model implies via isalpha on a single char, which fails for surrogate halves), astral endings come back unchanged. Either result sharply constrains whether the rule is 'isalpha + increment' or a BMP-only code-point check, and whether case is preserved for non-ASCII.

question: Does the advance rule apply to final characters that are letters only under Unicode case-folding/letter-category edge cases — specifically combining-letter-like and letter-number characters (Roman numeral Ⅳ, circled letter Ⓐ, modifier letter ʰ, superscript letter ⁿ, Roman numeral ⅰ) — and how does it advance them?
expect: If the rule is 'advance any Unicode letter by one code point', expect Ⅳ(U+2163)->Ⅴ(U+2164), Ⅰ(U+2160)->Ⅱ(U+2161), Ⓐ(U+24B6)->Ⓑ(U+24B7), ⓐ(U+24D0)->ⓑ(U+24D1), ʰ(U+02B0)->U+02B1, ⁿ(U+207F)->U+2080 (crossing into subscript digits), ⅰ(U+2170)->ⅱ(U+2171), ⅿ(U+217F)->U+2180 (crossing out of Roman numerals), and the a-prefixed ones likewise. If only 'true alphabetic' letters advance and letter-numbers/modifiers are left alone, those inputs come back unchanged — that would split str.isalpha() (which is True for Ⅳ, Ⓐ, ʰ, ⁿ) from the box's actual letter test.

question: Does the final-character advance rule also apply to letters in the Supplementary Multilingual Plane beyond the Deseret/Math ranges tested — e.g. U+1D400-range mathematical alphanumerics versus U+1E900-range Adlam letters — and does it increment by code point even when that crosses into a non-letter, and what happens at the BMP/SMP boundary for a final BMP letter like U+D7FB?
expect: If the rule is 'advance the final character by one Unicode code point whenever it is a letter', then U+1E900 (Adlam a) -> U+1E901, U+1E94F -> U+1E950, U+2C00 (Glagolitic) -> U+2C01, U+2C2F -> U+2C30, and U+1E900 preceded by anything still advances; if the rule is a fixed ASCII/Latin-only table, these stay unchanged or behave differently. Any non-letter result (e.g. crossing from a letter to a following non-letter code point) confirms pure code-point increment without letter-checking on the output.

question: When the final letter's code-point successor is a non-letter (e.g. 'z'->'{', 'Z'->'[', Greek/Cyrillic letters whose successor is punctuation or unassigned), does f still increment by code point, or does it wrap within the letter range like ASCII z->a?
expect: If f increments by code point unconditionally for letters, expect '{', '[', 'y{', 'a[', U+03CA (ω->ϊ), U+03AA (Ω->Ϊ), U+0450 (я->ѐ), U+0430 (Я->а), U+0431 (а->б), U+0102 (ā->Ă). If it wraps within letters like the ASCII z->a rule, expect 'a','A','ya','aA', and Greek/Cyrillic letters wrapping to the start of their alphabet (ω->α, Ω->Α, я->а). This distinguishes the two wrap hypotheses directly and probes whether the ASCII z->a behavior generalizes to non-ASCII.

question: Does the final-character advance apply to a letter whose successor is a non-letter but which is NOT at a script/block boundary — specifically letters followed by unassigned or symbol code points (e.g. Latin 'þ'->'ÿ' is fine, but what about 'ÿ'->U+0100 letter; and letters like U+024F, U+0374, U+0530, U+058F, U+1C80, U+2C2F tested) — and does f ever produce a non-letter successor, or does it wrap/skip to stay a letter?
expect: Each ends in a letter whose immediate successor is unassigned or a symbol/mark. If f increments by raw code point regardless (like E11's ω->ϊ, я->ѐ), outputs will be the +1 code points (many non-letters). If f wraps or skips to the next letter, we'll see jumps. Any deviation from +1 tells me whether the rule is 'increment if last char is a letter' vs 'increment and require result be a letter'.

question: When the final character is a letter whose code-point successor is a combining mark or other non-letter in the middle of a script block (e.g. Latin 'a'->'b' is fine, but what about letters immediately followed by combining diacritics or other marks, like U+0345 combining Greek ypogegrammeni, or letters like U+05D0 Hebrew alef whose successor U+05D1 is a letter but U+05EA tav->U+05EB unassigned), does f ever advance into a combining mark, and does it advance Hebrew/Arabic letters at all?
expect: If f advances any final Unicode letter by one code point, Hebrew alef U+05D0 -> U+05D1, tav U+05EA -> U+05EB (unassigned), Arabic alef U+0627 -> U+0628, yeh U+064A -> U+064B (a combining mark!), Devanagari U+0905 -> U+0906, U+0939 -> U+093A (combining), Thai U+0E01 -> U+0E02, U+0E2E -> U+0E2F (punctuation). If f restricts to letters with a letter successor, the U+064A, U+0939, U+0E2E cases would stay unchanged. If f only handles certain scripts, some would be unchanged. This tests whether the successor being a combining mark blocks the advance.

question: Does f advance the final character of an empty string or a string consisting only of non-letters, and does it ever change a string when the last character is a letter whose code-point successor is a surrogate code point or a noncharacter (e.g. U+D7FF, U+FFFE, U+FFFF), which the model currently leaves untouched?

question: Does f advance a final letter even when that letter is the last code point before a surrogate pair boundary or when the string itself ends in a lone low surrogate / reversed surrogate, and does it treat a final high surrogate followed by nothing as a non-letter?

question: Does f leave a string unchanged when the final character is a letter whose code-point successor is a non-letter that is NOT a surrogate/noncharacter — specifically the last letter before a block of combining marks or symbols (e.g. Latin/Greek letters immediately followed by combining diacritics), and does it advance into a combining mark or stop?

question: Does f advance a final letter whose code-point successor is a non-letter that is a combining mark or unassigned/format character specifically in the Latin Extended / IPA / combining-diacritics boundary regions, or does it stop at such boundaries — testing the edge cases where my model predicts a plain +1 increment but the box might instead refuse to advance into non-letter territory?

question: For a final non-ASCII letter whose +1 successor is a lone surrogate-range code point (U+D800–U+DFFF, not a valid character), does f still increment by one code point (producing an unpaired surrogate), or does it refuse/wrap/behave differently — a boundary the model has only tested via astral pairs, not a lone surrogate as the successor of a BMP letter?

question: Does f advance a final non-ASCII letter whose code-point successor is a combining mark (e.g. a letter immediately followed by U+0300-style combining diacritics), or does it treat combining-mark successors as a stopping boundary?

question: Does f advance a final non-ASCII letter by plain code-point +1 even when the successor is the first code point of a different Unicode plane boundary (U+FFFF -> U+10000) or the last BMP code point, and does it handle the astral successor correctly (surrogate pair) rather than refusing?

question: When the final character is a letter whose code-point successor is itself a letter but lies in a different case class (e.g. lowercase successor is uppercase, or vice versa), does f still just do code-point +1, or does it try to preserve case class by skipping to the next same-case letter?
